title: Leno: Movie Cars and a Truth Stranger Than Fiction

body_markdown:
The last Hagerty Drivers Club[issue about car movies](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) got my brain turning. We made fun of[some bad ones](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/leno-bad-car-movies-ive-loved/) in the last column, but there were some good ones, too. One of them was *Thunder Road* with Robert Mitchum. It came out in 1958, and I can still remember the song, actually sung by Robert Mitchum: “Let me tell the story, I can tell it all, about the mountain boy who ran illegal alcohol…” At one point, they open the hood of Mitchum’s car and you can see it’s a real ’50 Ford with a 239 flathead and all the trick stuff. I always like it when they at least try to make it look real, like it could have happened.


Another one that wasn’t a bad effort was *The Lively Set* , from 1964. Of course, I like it because it features the Chrysler Turbine car, but it also had Mickey Thompson and all the big racers back then. You see Thompson driving through the desert in a Galaxie and you can hear the car slamming down over the bumps, *bang!* and the Turbine car pulls ahead because it’s lighter, and that all sort of made sense. It also had a song, one by Bobby Darin, called “Look at Me,” which was co-written by Randy Newman when he was just a kid (Newman wrote some music for *Lost in Space* , all the *Toy Story* songs, etc., etc.). That was a real car movie with a real plot and also Pamela Tiffin. I still remember the scene where she goes behind the car door to change and you see her dress drop to the floor. All of us kids in the theater went “WHOA!”


Jay Leno's Garage


Then there were the TV shows with cars. I loved that they gave Jim Rockford the base-model Firebird in *The Rockford Files* . Yeah, it was a 400 underneath—[we actually had the car here on the show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzodibRsNu0) —but because he was supposed to be this broke guy, it made more sense that he would have the cheap model. I grew up in a little New England bump of a town where anything with less than four doors was like a Ferrari, so of course I watched *Route 66* for the Corvette. It wasn’t till I was an adult that I thought, “Hey, how come they’re always wearing fancy new clothes everywhere they stop? How much luggage can you put in a ’62 Corvette anyway?”


I don’t go for “celebrity ownership” cars, but I’ve got one that was in a few movies. The great Katharine Hepburn drove a Bugatti T38A in the 1933 film *Christopher Strong* , and the car appeared in a couple of other movies, including *The Gay Divorcee* with Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. The car is unique because it has a custom body made by Murphy in America, which makes it the only American-bodied Bugatti that we know of. Charles Howard was an early Buick dealer and race car owner, and he also owned the famous racing horse, *Seabiscuit* (Jeff Bridges played Howard in the Seabiscuit movie). Ettore Bugatti was hot to get a couple of Millers because he wanted to copy the top-end, so Howard traded him two Millers for a Bugatti chassis that was sent to Pasadena, where the Walter Murphy Company put a body on it. The car never left Los Angeles after that.


Originally it was supercharged and the supercharger was missing when I got it, so I was calling all over France trying to find one. One day I’m at a garage sale nearby held by a guy selling a lot of car parts, and I ask him if he’s got any superchargers. He goes, “Yeah, got one right here, came off a Bugatti.” It was the exact one! It had come off my car in the 1940s, and here it was at this garage sale. You couldn’t put that in a movie—nobody would believe it.
